clue.text: Win and celebrate

blocks.note: first meaning: a victory, as a noun
second meaning: to rejoice over success, as a verb

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a sports fan's instruction; the same word is a noun for the win and a verb for the celebrating.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a great victory and, as a verb, to exult or rejoice after succeeding.

clue.text: Punch's dog in play about bishop

indicators.note: about means going round, so one word wraps around the other

blocks.note: to play with something is to toy with it
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: Mr Punch's dog appears in a puppet play featuring a bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: In the traditional Punch and Judy puppet show, Punch has a dog called Toby.
explanation.definitionFit: Toby is the name of the dog in Punch and Judy, the British seaside puppet show.

clue.text: Appropriate batting line-up

blocks.note: first meaning: proper, acceptable
second meaning: the sequence in which cricketers bat is the batting order

explanation.walkthrough: A cricket side's batsmen go in according to the batting order, so a team arranged that way is lined up in sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means fitting or permissible, and also arranged in sequence, as a cricket team's batsmen are.

clue.text: Fly military aircraft across Germany and Spain

indicators.note: lying across something means stretching over it on both sides, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a MiG is a Russian military jet
D is the international vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: An order to pilot a warplane over Germany and Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: Fly looks like a verb telling you to pilot the aircraft; it is the noun, the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A midge is a tiny two-winged insect, an example of a fly.

clue.text: Sadness shown by audience coming from play

blocks.note: heartbreak is deep sorrow
a theatre's audience is the house, as in a full house

explanation.surface: Grief displayed by spectators leaving a theatre performance.
explanation.walkthrough: Heartbreak House is a 1919 play by George Bernard Shaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartbreak House is a play by George Bernard Shaw, so it is one example of a drama.

clue.text: Popular - word describing one caretaker

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so one word goes around another

blocks.note: in means fashionable, popular
a term is a word
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A popular term used to describe a caretaker.
explanation.walkthrough: Caretaker looks like a noun for a janitor, but it is the adjective, as in a caretaker government holding office temporarily.
explanation.definitionFit: A caretaker government or manager serves temporarily, which is what an interim one does.

clue.text: Saying last rites, talk so differently

indicators.note: saying the words differently means putting their letters in a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, all fifteen letters

explanation.surface: A priest is urged to phrase the last rites in another way.
explanation.walkthrough: Saying reads as a verb about speaking the rites; it is the noun, a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: It takes all sorts (to make a world) is a well-known proverb, a saying about tolerating different people.

clue.text: Main part, perhaps, I retell to comic

indicators.note: something comic is absurd and jumbled, so the letters come out in a funny new order

blocks.note: first part of the fodder
rest of the fodder

explanation.surface: An actor explains their lead role again to a comedian.
explanation.walkthrough: The word to does double duty in the fodder; comic is the signal, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The character named in a play's title, like Hamlet, is often the lead, hence perhaps the main part.

clue.text: Is lying in light rough that's deceiving

indicators.note: light suggests loose and unfixed, so the letters are not held in their order
lying inside something means sitting within it, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A golf ball sits in the light rough, which is deceptive.
explanation.walkthrough: Light rough sounds like the golf course's longer grass; the letters of rough are mixed and IS goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A rogue is a dishonest rascal, so roguish behaviour is tricky and deceiving.

clue.text: Old French president needing hand with job

blocks.note: mitt is slang for a hand
an errand is a small job

explanation.surface: A former French leader needs help with a task.
explanation.walkthrough: Need a hand looks like asking for help; hand is just the slang word for the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: François Mitterrand was President of France from 1981 to 1995.

clue.text: Report coarse players

blocks.note: broad humour is coarse or vulgar
the actors in a play are its cast

explanation.surface: A complaint filed about rude actors.
explanation.walkthrough: Report reads as a noun or a complaint; it is the verb, to transmit or make widely known.
explanation.definitionFit: To broadcast news is to transmit or spread it widely, a synonym of report.

clue.text: Awkward drunk

blocks.note: first meaning: difficult, as in a tricky situation
second meaning: intoxicated, informally

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like describing a clumsy drinker; the two words are separate meanings of one short adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A tight spot is an awkward one, and tight is informal slang for intoxicated.

clue.text: Commercial outlet in period before Christmas

blocks.note: an ad is an advertisement, a commercial
a vent is an opening for release, an outlet

explanation.surface: A shop that opens in the run-up to Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: Commercial outlet looks like a single phrase meaning a shop; it splits into the advertisement and the opening.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Christian calendar the weeks leading up to Christmas Day are the season called Advent.

clue.text: Viceroy, first to knock male club that's disreputable

indicators.note: first to means take only the opening letter of the next word

blocks.note: its first letter
he is the male pronoun
a dive is a seedy bar or nightclub

explanation.surface: A colonial governor knocks over a man in a seedy nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: The Khedive was the title of the Ottoman viceroy who governed Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: Khedive was the title of the viceroys who ruled Egypt on behalf of the Ottoman Sultan, 1867–1914.

clue.text: Rejected, we hear, in every part

indicators.note: what we hear is the sound of the words, not their spelling

blocks.note: to throw something out is to reject it

explanation.surface: Turned down, apparently, everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Throughout means all the way through, in every part of something.

clue.text: Poisonous plant, British, brought in by her boy

blocks.note: taken as written
B is the abbreviation for British
a boy's name

explanation.surface: A British poisonous plant is brought home by a woman's son.
explanation.walkthrough: Boy stands for any boy's name; the plant's name tells you which one.
explanation.definitionFit: Herb Christopher, or baneberry, is a woodland plant whose berries are toxic.

clue.text: A new chair vandalised, and crockery?

indicators.note: something vandalised is smashed up, so its letters end up rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder

explanation.surface: Vandals wreck a new chair, and the plates too?
explanation.definitionFit: Chinaware is porcelain tableware, such as plates and cups, which is what crockery means.

clue.text: Columbian one, one drunk very rarely

indicators.note: someone drunk staggers about, so these letters lurch into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, all fifteen letters

explanation.surface: A South American drinker is described as one who indulges only now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Drunk looks like a description of the Columbian; it is the signal to rearrange the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A blue moon is an uncommon extra full moon, so the idiom means hardly ever.

clue.text: Yorkshire river passing over a large crater

blocks.note: the Calder is a river in West Yorkshire
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire river flows over a huge hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, passing over means the river's name sits above the next piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A caldera is the vast basin left when a volcano collapses, a very large crater.

clue.text: Dance on stage, saving energy

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it held inside, so one short word encloses another

blocks.note: taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy
a stage in a process is a step

explanation.surface: Someone dances on stage while conserving their strength.
explanation.walkthrough: Stage reads as the theatre platform; here it means a phase. The energy goes inside on, and the phase follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-step is a ballroom dance popular in the early twentieth century.

clue.text: A giant, swine holding queue back

indicators.note: holding means having inside, so one word encloses another
back means the whole result is read from right to left

blocks.note: a hog is a pig
a tail is a line of people waiting, a queue

explanation.surface: A huge pig keeps a line of people back.
explanation.walkthrough: Goliath is the Philistine giant slain by David in the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Goliath is the biblical giant, and the name is used for any huge person.

clue.text: Say name of Island

blocks.note: to state is to say
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: An instruction to name an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Say name reads as an order to name something; it is two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Staten Island is one of New York City's five boroughs, an island in the harbour.

clue.text: Ready to drop a couple of lines home

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line, so two of them
at home means in

explanation.surface: A worker exhausted after writing a few lines at home.
explanation.walkthrough: Ready to drop looks like a delivery about to be made; it means utterly exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: All in is an informal idiom for completely exhausted, so tired one might collapse.

clue.text: This may turn up? Correct

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom of the grid to the top

blocks.note: the tide is said to turn

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about something turning up, then an answer: right.
explanation.walkthrough: The tide turns, so this may turn describes it; up in a down clue reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit a text is to revise and correct its errors.

clue.text: Love huge Greek character

blocks.note: love is a nil score in tennis, shaped like O
mega is slang for enormous

explanation.surface: Someone adores a big Greek personality.
explanation.walkthrough: Character suggests a person; it is a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, so it is a Greek character.

clue.text: Not connected by marriage, a Parisian's told

blocks.note: un is the French for a
to relate a story is to tell it

explanation.surface: A Parisian reports that two people are not in-laws.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after Parisian joins the pieces as is; told reads as a past verb meaning recounted.
explanation.definitionFit: People who are not kin, by blood or by marriage, are unrelated.

clue.text: Swing - net added to facility, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly points to how a word is heard rather than written

blocks.note: to net an animal is to trap it
facility means ease, skill without effort

explanation.surface: A swing with a safety net added to a fitness facility, so it is said.
explanation.walkthrough: Facility looks like a building; here it means ease of doing something.
explanation.definitionFit: A trapeze is a horizontal bar hung on ropes, a swing used by acrobats.

clue.text: Where youngsters play could make one spit, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: a mouthful of the stuff in it would make a child spit
setter's reading: the play area is full of the material a coastal spit is made of

explanation.surface: A children's play area where grit in the mouth makes you spit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites an anagram of one spit, which fails; the playful hint is that the word spit sits around 'and' in the answer, and a spit is a sand ridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandpit is a shallow box of sand where small children dig and play.
